items.title: Wouter van Balveren van OBGZ over minibiebs: “We hebben eigenlijk 350 vestigingen”
items.raw_text: In Nijmegen staan honderden minibiebs in de stad. De bibliotheek besloot niet te concurreren met deze kleine boekenkastjes die iedereen wel uit het straatbeeld herkent, maar juist te kijken wat ze voor elkaar kunnen betekenen. Wouter van Balveren, innovatiemanager bij OBGZ (Nijmegen en omstreken) vertelt hoe de samenwerking met de minibiebeigenaren ontstond, wat het oplevert en hoe je een samenwerking opzet. Kun je kort vertellen wat jullie met de minibiebs doen? “Minibiebs zijn natuurlijk al heel lang overal te vinden. Wij zagen ze ook om ons heen. Je kunt daar op twee manieren naar kijken. Je kunt het zien als een bedreiging en denken: dat is niet wat wij als bibliotheek zijn. Wij hebben een actuele, zorgvuldig samengestelde collectie. Wat heb je dan aan zo’n minibieb? Maar je kunt het ook anders bekijken. Het zijn enthousiaste mensen die van lezen houden en het leuk vinden om boeken en verhalen met anderen te delen. In die zin zijn het eigenlijk ambassadeurs van leesplezier, net als wij. Daarnaast past het goed bij onze missie: wij staan voor leesplezier, verhalen en toegang tot boeken voor iedereen. Daar sluiten de minibiebs perfect op aan.’ We zijn de minibiebs steeds meer gaan zien als een soort opstap naar de bibliotheek. Wij proberen natuurlijk met onze vestigingen in allerlei wijken zichtbaar te zijn. Maar minibiebs zitten echt in de haarvaten van de samenleving. items.title: Bouw je eigen AI-assistent: van losse prompts naar een digitale collega
items.raw_text: Veel mensen gebruiken AI als vraagbaak: je start een chat, stelt een vraag, krijgt antwoord en begint de volgende keer weer met een nieuwe chat. Een AI-assistent oftewel een ‘custom agent’ werkt net anders: het is een digitale collega die je inwerkt op een specifieke taak. De grootste winst? Die ligt in het automatiseren van repeterende werkzaamheden, zodat er meer tijd overblijft voor strategie, creativiteit en contact met jouw doelgroep. In dit artikel lees je wat een AI-assistent is en hoe je er zelf een kunt inrichten om efficiënter te kunnen werken. Wat is een AI-assistent? Een AI-assistent kun je inrichten om een specifieke taak zo goed mogelijk uit te voeren. In plaats van bij iedere nieuwe chat opnieuw uit te leggen wat je wilt, geef je de assistent vooraf context, instructies en relevante documenten mee. Daardoor begrijpt het programma jouw werkwijze beter en kan het jou consistenter en beter ondersteunen. De AI voert geen autonome taken uit zoals een AI-agent, maar werkt alleen met jouw input. Waar te beginnen? Het kan ingewikkeld klinken, maar om een assistent te kunnen inrichten hoef je geen ICT- of programmeringskennis te hebben. Vrijwel alle AI-platformen bieden de mogelijkheid om een eigen assistent te bouwen. Hierbij is de start het meest belangrijk: een AI-assistent is namelijk zo slim als de informatie waarmee je hem voedt. items.title: Zó geef je een landelijke campagne een lokale online boost

items.title: Creatief met Canva: 8 slimme manieren om tijd te besparen
items.raw_text: Als contentmaker bij een bibliotheek ben je continu aan het schakelen. Je werkt aan de contentstrategie, ontwerpt materialen, verwerkt interne verzoeken en zorgt ervoor dat alles op tijd gepubliceerd wordt. Ondertussen blijft de agenda zich vullen met nieuwe activiteiten, workshops en campagnes. De online ontwerptool Canva kan daarbij een goede hulp zijn om tijd te besparen. items.title: Kleine stappen, groot verschil: efficiënt aan de slag met digitale toegankelijkheid
items.raw_text: Veel bibliotheken zijn aan de slag met digitale toegankelijkheid. Vaak deels omdat je intrinsiek gemotiveerd bent om er voor iedereen te zijn, deels omdat het moet van de wet digitale toegankelijkheid. Toch kan het in de waan van de dag een uitdaging zijn om stappen te zetten. Gelukkig kan je al veel kleine dingen aanpassen in je routine, die een groot verschil maken op lange termijn. In dit artikel laat ik zien hoe je efficiënte stappen zet en slim werkt aan de digitale toegankelijkheid van jouw bibliotheek. Opfrissen Wil je even een opfrisser wat digitale toegankelijkheid inhoudt en waarom je hiermee aan de slag wil en moet? Lees dan het artikel Wat levert een digitaal toegankelijke bibliotheek op? Gebruik bijvoorbeeld de praatplaat om het gesprek hierover op gang te brengen. items.title: Acht nieuwe trainees zijn van start
items.raw_text: Op 1 september starten 8 nieuwe trainees met het Traineeship Openbare Bibliotheken. De komende 2 jaar werken zij bij verschillende bibliotheken in Noord- en Zuid-Holland aan actuele vraagstukken én aan hun eigen professionele en persoonlijke ontwikkeling. Het is alweer de derde lichting trainees die starten aan Probiblio’s traineeprogramma. Tijdens het traineeship werken de trainees in 3 periodes van 8 maanden bij verschillende bibliotheken. Vier dagen per week werken zij mee binnen de organisatie. Dat kan zijn vanuit een gerichte opdracht, waarbij de trainee zelfstandig aan een concreet vraagstuk werkt en een resultaat oplevert, maar ook als meewerkende professional in een team, bijvoorbeeld als tijdelijke vervanging of extra versterking. Daarnaast volgen de trainees een gezamenlijk ontwikkelprogramma met human skills-trainingen, vakinhoudelijke trainingen, intervisie en coaching. Zo doen zij brede praktijkervaring op én ontwikkelen zij zich verder als professional. Ook Marit Thoen, die tijdens de vorige lichting vanaf de tweede opdracht instroomde, blijft nog acht maanden langer aan Probiblio verbonden. Zij start een derde opdracht bij de OBA. Daarmee zijn er vanaf september negen trainees actief bij negen verschillende opdrachten. items.title: Resultaten nulmeting Provinciaal Collectiebeleidsplan
items.raw_text: Dit jaar zijn we in Noord- en Zuid-Holland gestart met de implementatie van het Provinciaal Collectiebeleidsplan. Als onderdeel daarvan wordt voor alle negen thema’s een nulmeting uitgevoerd. Voor zes thema’s is deze inmiddels door vrijwel alle bibliotheken ingevuld. In deze blog bespreken we de belangrijkste uitkomsten. Drie thema’s centraal in 2027 Op basis van de uitkomsten van de vragenlijsten en de vragen die wij binnenkrijgen, is besloten dat volgend jaar de focus ligt op drie thema’s: doelgroepgericht collectioneren, jongeren en plek. Deze thema’s krijgen volgend jaar een publicatiepagina op de website en extra aanbod. De andere thema’s krijgen ook aandacht, maar zijn geen focuspunt. items.title: Lezen dichter bij studenten: de kracht van samenwerken
items.raw_text: Zeven schoolbibliotheken op zeven locaties. Dat is het doel van de samenwerking tussen ROC van Twente, vier Overijsselse bibliotheken en Rijnbrink. Op maandag 7 september werd de eerste Bibliotheek op school officieel geopend bij ROC-locatie Wierdensestraat in Almelo. Een mooi voorbeeld van hoe bovenlokale samenwerking lezen dichter bij studenten kan brengen. En van hoe we ze samen veel meer bijbrengen dan een vak. Erwin Karst was als adviseur bij Rijnbrink aanjager van deze bovenlokale samenwerking. Een proces van meerdere jaren, met veel gesprekken, voorlichtingen en workshops om opleidingen en docenten mee te krijgen. Een goed teken, ook gezien recent onderzoek waaruit blijkt dat de leesvaardigheid onder Nederlandse scholieren verder daalt . En dat houdt meer in dan een kast vol boeken. De Bibliotheek op school aanpak draait om het creëren van een omgeving waarin lezen een vanzelfsprekende plek krijgt. items.title: Hoe doorbreek je de cirkel van laaggeletterdheid? 7 tips
items.raw_text: Een kind dat er lekker op los kletst, samen met papa en mama boekjes leest en zich goed kan uitdrukken. En ouders die trots toekijken, want hoe anders was hun eigen jeugd… Gezinsgericht werken aan basisvaardigheden levert meer op dan goede ontwikkelkansen. items.title: Caribische bibliotheken versterken samenwerking tijdens uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador
items.raw_text: Hoe bouw je samen aan een sterk netwerk van bibliotheken, terwijl je ook over grenzen heen van elkaar blijft leren? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens een bijzondere uitwisselingsweek in El Salvador. Bibliotheken uit het Caribisch deel van ons Koninkrijk kwamen samen om kennis en ervaringen met elkaar te delen en om een belangrijke stap te zetten in hun gezamenlijke ontwikkeling. Tijdens de conferentie ondertekenden Biblioteka Nashonal Kòrsou , Biblioteca Nacional Aruba , Biblioteka Públiko Boneiru , Sint Maarten Library , Gertrude Judson Bicentennial Public Library St. Eustatius en Queen Wilhelmina Library hun gezamenlijke netwerkplan. Daarmee bekrachtigen zij hun gedeelde ambities en afspraken voor de komende periode. Een netwerk met ambitie De Caribische bibliotheken werken, met begeleiding van Common Eye , aan een sterk en duurzaam netwerk dat aansluit bij hun eigen behoeften, ervaringen en ambities. Het netwerkplan richt zich onder andere op een sterkere positionering van de Caribische bibliotheken en de ontwikkeling van toekomstbestendige bibliotheken. Als kennis- en expertisepartner zijn wij vanuit Rijnbrink, samen met de Koninklijke Bibliotheek (KB) , betrokken bij het netwerk. We ondersteunen de bibliotheken bij hun organisatorische en inhoudelijke ontwikkeling en helpen mee om de ambities uit het netwerkplan verder te brengen. items.title: Hoe de VoorleesExpress gezinnen versterkt en bibliotheken scherper laat werken

Al jarenlang werken bibliotheken, vrijwilligers en samenwerkingspartners aan een voorleesritueel bij gezinnen: voor taalplezier, taalontwikkeling én gelijke kansen. items.title: Prentenboeken in Papiamentu: een feest van herkenning
items.raw_text: Een prentenboek vertalen lijkt eenvoudig: je zet de ene taal om in de andere. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat een kind zich écht herkent in een verhaal? Voor de nieuwe Papiamentu-prentenboeken – gerealiseerd in het project Leesbevordering in meertalige gezinnen – dachten leden van de klankbordgroep mee over taal, cultuur en geschiedenis. Waarom is de keuze voor opa beter dan de officiële vertaling tawela? Waarom mocht het verhaal van Tula in de nieuwe prentenboekencollectie niet ontbreken? En wat gebeurt er als een kind voor het eerst een verhaal in zijn eigen taal hoort? Jakeema, Myrthe en Margriet vertellen hoe juist die keuzes het verschil maken. Waarom vertalen nodig was Zoals het eerdere artikel over dit project al aangaf: voorlezen stimuleert de taalontwikkeling van jonge kinderen het beste. Juist voorlezen in de thuistaal, de taal van het hart, levert veel extra’s op. Ouders op Bonaire willen dat met alle liefde doen, vertelt Jakeema Hernandez, programmaleider bij Bibliotheek Bonaire. Maar de collectie prentenboeken in het Papiamentu is beperkt. Jakeema is dan ook blij met de nieuwe, vertaalde Papiamentu-boeken. Als kind hield ik al van lezen, maar een boek in mijn eigen taal vinden in de boekhandel of bibliotheek was onmogelijk. Voor mijn inner child is het mooi om te zien dat er nu boeken in het Papiamentu bestaan. items.title: Privacy & informatiebeveiliging: dit speelt er in de bibliotheek

items.title: Voorlezen in de taal van je hart: meer verhalen in Farsi en Papiamentu

items.title: Haal meer uit data voor maatschappelijke programmering met de Datateam®methode
items.raw_text: Hoe maak je keuzes rond programmering die niet alleen goed voelen, maar ook goed onderbouwd zijn? Die vraag stond centraal tijdens de inspirerende en energieke workshop Haal meer uit data – De Datateam®methode op 4 juni bij Kunstwerk! in Zevenaar. Dertien bibliotheekmedewerkers uit Gelderland en Overijssel maakten kennis met de Datateam®methode. Universiteit Twente ontwikkelde deze aanpak, die organisaties helpt om maatschappelijke vraagstukken data-geïnformeerd aan te pakken. Onder begeleiding van Maaike Korte (Expertis) ontdekten deelnemers hoe data, samenwerking en een gestructureerde werkwijze kunnen bijdragen aan betere keuzes en sterkere programmering. Benieuwd naar wat deze workshop opleverde? Wij zetten de belangrijkste inzichten voor je op een rijtje. Bijvoorbeeld: hoe bereik je als bibliotheek beter de NT1-doelgroep met je huidige aanbod? In kleine groepen verkenden zij de eerste stappen van de Datateam®methode. items.title: HR Actueel – Mogelijke afschaffing compensatie transitievergoeding: wat betekent dit voor bibliotheken?
items.raw_text: Vanaf 2027 ontvangen werkgevers mogelijk geen compensatie meer voor de transitievergoeding bij ontslag wegens langdurige arbeidsongeschiktheid. Dat heeft het kabinet aangekondigd. Hoewel de parlementaire behandeling nog loopt, is het voor bibliotheken en cultuurorganisaties verstandig om nu alvast inzicht te krijgen in de mogelijke gevolgen. Extra kosten bij langdurig verzuim Langdurig verzuim brengt al aanzienlijke kosten met zich mee. Denk aan twee jaar loondoorbetaling, re-integratietrajecten, arbodienstverlening en vervanging van medewerkers. Als de compensatieregeling verdwijnt, komen daar mogelijk ook de kosten van de transitievergoeding volledig bij. De financiële impact kan aanzienlijk zijn. Een medewerker met twintig dienstjaren en een bruto maandsalaris van € 3.500 heeft bijvoorbeeld recht op een transitievergoeding van ruim € 23.000. Zonder compensatie zijn deze kosten volledig voor rekening van de werkgever. Daarmee wordt langdurig verzuim niet alleen een HR-vraagstuk, maar ook een belangrijk onderwerp voor directie, management, begroting en risicomanagement. Aandacht voor slapende dienstverbanden Ook de discussie rondom slapende dienstverbanden kan opnieuw relevanter worden. items.title: De tanden in een meerjarenplan

items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. Sommigen bepleiten ‘radicale openbaarheid’, wat simpelweg neerkomt op álles openbaar maken. items.title: Juli
items.raw_text: Online radicalisering van jongeren: het gesprek gaat door Deze maand is er opnieuw veel aandacht voor schadelijke en gewelddadige online netwerken. De NOS berichtte op 23 juli over de aanhouding van een jonge man die wordt verdacht van deelname aan een sadistisch Com-netwerk ofwel community. Binnen dergelijke besloten online groepen kunnen kwetsbare jongeren worden geronseld en aangezet tot zelfbeschadiging, misbruik en geweld. De actuele berichtgeving raakt direct aan de onderwerpen die op 22 juni centraal stonden tijdens het symposium Online radicalisering van jongeren: herkennen, begrijpen en handelen, georganiseerd door de ATKM, de NCTV en ECP. Onder leiding van dagvoorzitter Liesbeth Rasker gingen professionals, onderzoekers en ervaringsdeskundigen in gesprek over de vraag hoe online radicalisering tijdig kan worden herkend, zonder jongeren te snel te veroordelen of te stigmatiseren. Radicalisering begint vaak niet met een uitgesproken ideologie of een duidelijke intentie om geweld te gebruiken. Het kan beginnen bij menselijke vragen: wie ben ik, waar hoor ik bij en wie neemt mij serieus? Online groepen kunnen daarop inspelen en grenzen tussen humor, provocatie, uitsluiting en geweld geleidelijk laten vervagen. De rode draad in het symposium, de podcast en de actuele berichtgeving is daarom dezelfde: blijf nieuwsgierig, investeer in kennis van de online leefwereld en voer het gesprek voordat standpunten en gedrag verder verharden. items.title: Zomerblog Marjolijn Bonthuis
items.raw_text: “Worden we een museum?” Een persoonlijke zomerse beschouwing over Europa, AI en de stap van dialoog naar daadkracht Deze zomer lees ik Grand Hotel Europa van Ilja Leonard Pfeijffer. Het hotel in de roman staat symbool voor Europa: prachtig, rijk aan verhalen, maar vooral gericht op het verleden. Europa bewaart zijn kunst, architectuur en geschiedenis — en verkoopt die aan toeristen. Ondertussen wordt de toekomst elders gebouwd. Die gedachte dringt zich ook op wanneer ik kijk naar de huidige technologische ontwikkelingen. Terwijl Amerikaanse en Chinese bedrijven miljarden investeren in kunstmatige intelligentie, chips en digitale infrastructuur, zijn wij in Europa vaak vooral bezig met regels, risico’s en bescherming. Laat ik daar duidelijk over zijn: die aandacht is nodig. Zeker vanuit mijn dagelijkse verantwoordelijkheid voor digitale veiligheid, weerbaarheid en vertrouwen weet ik hoe belangrijk het is dat technologie niet zonder grenzen wordt ontwikkeld en toegepast. Big Tech heeft inmiddels zoveel economische, technologische en maatschappelijke macht opgebouwd dat stevige publieke kaders onvermijdelijk zijn. Bescherming van grondrechten, democratische controle en eerlijke concurrentie zijn geen luxe. Maar regels alleen maken ons nog geen speler. Als Europa vooral vastlegt onder welke voorwaarden technologie van anderen hier mag worden gebruikt, terwijl we zelf onvoldoende investeren in de ontwikkeling ervan, blijft onze invloed beperkt. items.title: Stichting ECP wijzigt structuur governance om ook in de toekomst bijdrage te kunnen leveren aan de digitale samenleving
items.raw_text: Om waarde te kunnen blijven toevoegen aan de digitale samenleving heeft Stichting ECP haar governance structuur aangepast. Eerder meldde Stichting ECP al dat ze de aanpassing aan het eind van dit jaar wil hebben ingericht, als uitkomst van een traject dat in 2024 in gang is gezet. Stichting ECP is er van overtuigd met deze governance structuur ook in de toekomst haar bijdrage te kunnen leveren via haar activiteiten en in samenwerking met het brede netwerk van publieke en private partijen die zich hiervoor inzetten. Een overzicht van wijzigingen governance en inrichting Stichting ECP is aan het einde van dit bericht opgenomen. items.title: IFLA September Townhall Meeting: Recording Available
items.raw_text: A recording from IFLA’s Townhall meetings on 8 and 10 September 2026 can be viewed on IFLA’s YouTube channel . Chaired by IFLA President Leslie Weir and Secretary General Sharon Memis, the meeting presented IFLA’s Sustainable Futures Journey . Complementing our existing Strategy, this looks less at ‘what’ IFLA is doing, and more at ‘how’, with a strong focus on our models for membership, volunteering and the finances for our Congress. While it is ambitious to look at all of these areas at once, it is also necessary in order to take a comprehensive appraoch to IFLA’s sustainability and effectiveness into our secodn century. You’re encouraged to share your views on our volunteer model via our survey , open until 30 September. They also noted the new page on our website with relevant information about our work with SIGL . Leslie and Sharon then talked about IFLA100 , our centenary, which was formally launched during our most recent Congress in Busan. This was both an opportunity to celebrate the people and moments that have shaped our field and Federation today, but also to reflect on the role and shape of international librarianship today and into the future. There are guides on what IFLA’s volunteer units and members and affiliates can do, and we encourage engagement in our Great IFLA100 Futures Challenge . items.title: Building Leadership Through Associations: A Conversation with Loida Garcia-Febo
items.raw_text: How can library associations strengthen leadership and help library and information professionals respond to increasingly complex and uncertain environments? On 25 June 2026, Loida Garcia-Febo, Chair of the IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) , joined a conversation with Roxana Huaman Huriarte, Chair of the IFLA Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Division , and Nick Boxem, Chair of the IFLA Europe Regional Division , both members of the IFLA Regional Council leadership group. The conversation explored leadership within IFLA and library associations, and how strategic planning, capacity building and professional networks can help organisations and individuals respond more effectively to change. Leadership is a capacity that can be developed Leadership is not simply linked to holding a formal position but it is a capacity that can be intentionally developed through experience, training, mentoring, coaching and opportunities to work with others. For library associations, this means creating environments where current and emerging leaders can learn, test ideas, build confidence and develop the skills required to guide organisations through change. Garcia-Febo highlighted the importance of leadership training, mentoring and coaching, alongside team building and effective communication. items.title: IFLA Europe Regional Division Webinar 2026: How EURDC supports Libraries across Europe
items.raw_text: The IFLA Europe Regional Division invites library professionals, information specialists, and IFLA members from across Europe to an engaging online webinar on 1 October 2026 at 11:00 CEST . Over the past five years, the Europe Regional Division Committee (EURDC) has worked to strengthen collaboration, advocacy, and engagement among libraries and library professionals throughout Europe. Despite these efforts, many colleagues remain unfamiliar with the division’s mandate, activities, and opportunities for involvement. This webinar aims to change that. During the session, four members of the current EURDC Committee, representing Finland, Germany, Norway, and Portugal, will introduce the division’s work and share practical examples of how EURDC supports the European library community. Participants will gain insights into the division’s objectives, ongoing initiatives, and future priorities. The webinar will also provide an opportunity for dialogue. Attendees will be encouraged to share their expectations, discuss challenges facing libraries in Europe, and suggest ways in which EURDC can better support their work and professional communities. The event will be conducted in English via Zoom, with automated subtitles available to improve accessibility. items.title: The Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) WLIC 2026 Outcomes Report
items.raw_text: Part of MLAS Members and Attendees at MLAS Business Meeting in Busan The IFLA Management of Library Associations Section (MLAS) had an active and substantive presence at the IFLA World Library and Information Congress (WLIC) 2026 in Busan. Activities included the MLAS Business Meeting, MLAS Open Session, IFLA Associations Meeting, an informal meeting of International Relations Chairs, and opportunities for congress attendees to connect with the MLAS Chair at the IFLA exhibition booth. Across these activities, common priorities emerged: strategic renewal, member engagement, leadership, partnerships, advocacy, financial sustainability, visibility, digital transformation and AI, resilience, crisis preparedness, and responsiveness to changing societal needs. These priorities are closely aligned with MLAS’s mission to support strong, well-managed library associations through leadership, peer learning, resource development, and effective association practices worldwide. Strong library associations do not simply have strategies. They make their strategies visible, translate them into action, engage their members, build partnerships, advocate effectively, develop new leaders, sustain their organisations, and continually renew themselves in response to change. items.title: IFLA President’s Message – August 2026
items.raw_text: The below message has been distributed to IFLA members and volunteers in all IFLA languages. I am writing to you today, still trying to get my feet back on the ground after an amazing time at our World Library and Information Congress in Busan . This was my first time attending as President! I will admit that I lost count of the number of meetings, speeches and other events I was involved in, but know that each one reinforced my excitement about libraries and our Federation. I will also admit to some pride in my gong technique. I want to begin by highlight the incredible winners of our awards this year, as well as our IFLA Medal and Scroll of Appreciation recipients. Thank you for all you do in support of libraries, our profession and IFLA. It was inspiring to see the extent to which political decision-makers in Korea both understand the potential of libraries and support libraries in realizing their potential. It is a situation we can all aspire to! It was such a pleasure to have an opportunity to talk individually with so many of you attending the Congress, whether members, volunteers or stakeholders, to thank you for your incredible support and friendship. I am sorry that I couldn’t connect personally with everyone, but I do hope that you are already putting our Congress next year in London in your diaries. items.title: The Great IFLA100 Futures Challenge
items.raw_text: Join us on the first stage of our drive to engage the global library field in a reflection on the future(s) of our institutions, our place in society, and our international cooperation. A key pillar of the programme for IFLA’s centenary year – IFLA100 – is a focus on the future. Alongside the remembering and celebration of our past achievements and the people that made them possible, we want this year to be a chance to build up the skills, attitudes and connections necessary to enter into our second century with confidence. Central to this is our work to build up the habit of futures thinking across our profession. This enables us to steer a path between a denialism driven by passivity, and an excessive reliance on specific predictions that leaves little room to react to the unexpected. IFLA already has a strong record of work in this space. Our Trend Report in 2024 shared a set of potential trends, as well as using these to offer a range of potential scenarios for the future, ready to be used by libraries and library workers to test their own plans. Our Weak Signals report added to this, using ideas gathered at the 2025 World Library and Information Congress to identify phenomena that could potentially have a transformative effect in the future. At our 2026 Congress, the keynote speech by Sohail Inayatullah provided further insights into techniques for futures thinking, complementing the keynote given by Riel Miller at our Toronto meetings in April. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. More than two-thirds of this year’s 15 selections are renovations or adaptive reuse projects. Libraries of all types are finding ways to acknowledge historical and environmental realities, embrace natural elements and cultural identities, evolve traditions, and build in flexibility to account for the unexpected. Read on for snapshots of these communities in motion. Natural immersion Maplewood (N.J.) Memorial Library Adjacent to a historic park, with protected natural areas on all sides, this 1955 masonry structure had nowhere to expand but up. The new, light-filled second floor features bird-safe glass, wood battens, and green roofs for a treehouse feel. The all-electric building, the first LEED Gold–certified library in New Jersey, includes solar panels that offset more than half of the library’s energy use. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. items.title: Newsmaker: Min Jin Lee
items.raw_text: Min Jin Lee has notched career milestones that few authors reach. Her immigration saga Pachinko was both a National Book Award finalist and a New York Times Top 10 Best Book of 2017, and it was adapted into a television series of the same name for Apple TV. Lee is also a Guggenheim fellow and the first Korean American to hold the role of New York State author laureate. Her latest title, American Hagwon (Cardinal, September), examines the influence of Korean “cram schools” among families in the Korean diaspora. American Libraries spoke with Lee ahead of her appearance at the American Library Association’s 2026 Annual Conference and Exhibition in Chicago. She discussed her new book, the library that shaped her, and her antidote to book bans. What inspired you to focus on the education system as it relates to the movements of a middle-class Korean American family in American Hagwon ? My research process involved all these interviews—I’ve done hundreds of them, probably almost 1,000 at this point—and every single time I talked to somebody, they would mention their education path. It was such an important and controversial subject. I thought, if I had to think about the most important value for Koreans, especially in the diaspora, what would I write about? Education turned out to be a beast, because people have lots of feelings about it. In the book, the Koh family loses wealth and status as they weather betrayal and financial crises. items.title: Mall Wonder
items.raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. items.title: Dismantling Disinformation
items.raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges. items.title: A Sense of Purpose
items.raw_text: When it comes to building resilient and equitable communities, libraries are natural leaders. We provide places where neighbors meet, learn, and support one another; where sustainability education becomes action; and where residents can find year-round climate refuge. When communities are resilient, they are better able to overcome barriers. The Obama Presidential Center (OPC) branch of Chicago Public Library (CPL) is an example of a library that strengthens the social infrastructure that underpins resilience. CPL Commissioner Chris Brown describes the branch as a civic platform for residents, artists, educators, and organizations to cocreate the life of the library and its surrounding public spaces. Though just 5,000 square feet, OPC was designed to spark connection, invite conversation, and inspire activities that encourage ­socialization and enjoyment. The branch partners with such nonprofits as the Art Institute of Chicago, the literary arts group StoryStudio Chicago , and the artist-led alt_Chicago . OPC is a striking example of how libraries do not just serve resilient communities, they help create them. On the Gulf Coast, sustainability is a daily requirement. Lindsay Cronk, dean of Tulane University Libraries in New Orleans, has shared that the library’s partnership with Keep Louisiana Beautiful , a state program, helps connect students, faculty, and staff with opportunities for conservation, beautification, recycling, and environmental action. items.title: Report: “As Digital Checkouts Soar, Los Angeles Libraries Pivot to AI Education”
items.raw_text: From the Yale Daily News Beyond fighting misinformation, public libraries are stepping up to bridge paywalls. While students often run into paid barriers when accessing articles via Google or Google Scholar, public libraries subscribe to expensive digital databases, academic journals, and major news outlets — including the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal — to provide free access to local students. Still, many students have been reluctant to get help from the librarians. “It’s quite common that when they come to this desk to ask a question, they say to me, ‘Oh, I’m really sorry to bother you,’” Charles [a Young Adult Librarian in LAPL’s Teen’scape department] said. “It’s not a bother — that’s literally the whole reason us librarians are here to help.” As students turn more and more from the paper pages to the digital screens of their research materials, physical library areas are not only continuing to exist, but actively evolving to meet the needs of new research methods. items.raw_text: The article linked below was recently published by College & Research Libraries (C&RL) Title Evolving Trends : A Bibliometric Analysis of Academic Librarians’ Publications at Twelve AAU Member Universities Authors Pete E. Pascuzzi Purdue University Libraries Jason B. Reed Purdue University Libraries Greenley Goedde Creech Purdue University Libraries Source College & Research Libraries Vol 87, No 5 (2026) Vol 87, No 5 (2026) Abstract The goal of this bibliometric study was to explore the broader publication patterns of academic librarians in both information and library science (ISLS) and interdisciplinary research for the years 2009 to 2023. Web of Science data were collected for 12 academic libraries. The results showed that while the number of ISLS publications has dropped, interdisciplinary publications have increased dramatically with a broad range of disciplines represented, and that collaborations in the medical sciences were a major contributor to this increase. The study suggests that some academic libraries have shifted their priorities over the past 15 years and that the assessment of libraries’ scholarly publications must evolve to capture this shift. items.title: Disclosing AI Use in Academic Research, a New Global Study From Oxford University Press
items.raw_text: Published today by Oxford University Press (OUP): We have updated our author and editor guidelines on the responsible, appropriate, and transparent use of AI, including a policy outlining what AI use should be disclosed when preparing manuscripts for our journals. In a recent global survey of more than 2,600 researchers, nearly three-quarters (74%) of respondents revealed they were unclear what AI use they should disclose, despite there being strong support for disclosure. With 44% of researchers concerned that disclosing their use of AI will negatively impact how others view their work, and only 36% recording their AI use during their research, our survey emphasizes the growing gap between AI use and disclosure in academic research, and recognizes the need for clear disclosure policies. Direct to Full Text Report (59 pages; PDF) Selected Findings From the Survey: 64% of researchers report AI as beneficial to their research, with over two-thirds (68%) using AI chatbots on the open web for their research, and just under half (49%) using machine translation. AI tools are most commonly used for discovering existing research (55%), summarizing existing research (46%), and editing the write-up of research (45%). Many (68%) agree that AI tools can reduce accessibility barriers, too. However, 35% of those in the arts and humanities never use AI tools in their research, as opposed to 15% and 18% for STM and the social sciences, respectively. items.title: Report: “DOJ Official Queried a Dozen Journals on ‘Partisan’ Views in 2025”
items.raw_text: From FYI Science Policy News: FYI Science Policy News obtained the letters through a July 2025 public records request. The new materials reveal a campaign spearheaded by then-interim US attorney for the District of Columbia Ed Martin to pressure publications prominent in the public health response to the COVID pandemic and in reproductive medicine. items.title: New Freckle Project Report Examines 15 Years of Public Library Use
items.raw_text: From EveryLibrary Institute: A new Freckle Project Report, “15 Years of IMLS Figures” , looks at national public library statistics from 2010 through 2024 and identifies a striking contrast: American public libraries have more facilities, more staff, and higher levels of funding than at any point in the period examined, while several major measures of physical library use remain substantially below their 2010 levels. The Freckle Project is led by researcher Tim Coates, and its publication is supported by the EveryLibrary Institute. The August 2026 Report examines 15 years of data from the Institute of Museum and Library Services on America’s public libraries. In 2024, the United States had 17,580 public library facilities and 147,289 library employees, while public libraries received nearly $18 billion for operations and another $1.6 billion for capital expenditures. Yet annual visits declined from approximately 1.57 billion in 2010 to 869 million in 2024, while total circulation fell from approximately 2.47 billion to 1.71 billion. Coates’s analysis highlights an especially significant decline in adult physical circulation. After subtracting electronic and children’s circulation from total circulation, he estimates that this category fell approximately 68 percent between 2010 and 2024. Title Accountability, Integrity: AI Policy in Public Libraries Authors Kathryn FitzGerald University of Washington Benjamin Lee University of Washington Source Public Library Quarterly DOI: 1 0.1080/01616846.2026.2725502 Abstract As artificial intelligence reshapes both library work and the information environment, public libraries must determine whether or how to engage with AI while maintaining library values. items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.raw_text: I arrived at my first Public Library Association Conference expecting to leave with organized notes, a clear list of takeaways, and practical ideas to share with colleagues. Instead, I left with a notebook full of starred ideas, half-written thoughts, and questions scribbled in the margins. Looking back, those messy notes reveal the sessions that stayed with me long after the conference ended. Conversations about internal communication, programming for older adults, and flexible, community-centered services challenged my assumptions and sparked new ideas for my own work. Sessions including “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications,” “Aging Together: Library Programming for Older Adults,” and “Memory Cafes in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections” reframed how I think about serving both staff and patrons. Ideas I Starred One of the most memorable concepts came from “Becoming One Library: How to Build Better Internal Communications.” Mary Kapusta described how her library system developed clearer, more intentional communication practices, including a framework called “Skim, Swim, Dive.” The model structures communication so staff can quickly identify key information and then choose how deeply they engage based on their needs and available time. The idea resonated with me because it recognizes a reality every workplace faces: staff absorb information differently, have varying capacities, and don’t need every message delivered in the same format. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content. items.title: One Year Later: The Digital Equity Act Cancellation and Libraries
items.raw_text: May 8, 2026, marked the one-year anniversary of the Trump Administration’s cancellation of the Digital Equity Act (DEA). The $2.75 billion Digital Equity Act was a part of a coordinated effort to provide communities across the U.S. with high-speed broadband and the skills and technology needed to thrive in our increasingly digital world. Libraries and other community anchor institutions were integral to the planning of this once-in-a-generation opportunity to address the digital divide. Collectively, these groups spent precious resources and staff time applying for DEA program grants, leading related coalition building efforts, and conducting outreach and asset mapping. The abrupt cancellation of the DEA grants last year was a significant blow to digital inclusion programs nationwide, impacting millions of Americans. According to the Idaho Commission for Libraries , over 80% of the state’s DEA Capacity Grant award “was slated for subgrants supporting rural Idahoans, including older adults and veterans.” Public and tribal libraries across the state would have benefited from grants to replace outdated computers to offer public training on cybersecurity and technology use. In Maine, nearly 130,000 people would have been directly served by DEA-funded programs, such as digital skills training, technical support, telehealth access, and affordable device programs. items.title: Rennie McDougall On How Social And Historical Forces Molded Twentieth Century Dance
items.raw_text: Rennie McDougall ‘s Nonstop Bodies: How Dance Shaped New York City gives readers a thrilling new perspective on twentieth century New York City by investigating the different choreographers, dancers, and dance movements that flourished there during that time. McDougall guides the reader through various dance movements, from the marathon dances of the Prohibition era to the Lindy Hop to the Rockettes and beyond. All the while, he catalogues the dense web of lineages that developed among specific dances and artists, allowing readers to see relationships among disparate dance forms that might not be immediately apparent. McDougall also dives into how social and historical forces directly molded the evolving dance forms, and the unique position New York City held to create countless connections between dancers and choreographers not only in the moment, but across time as well. Critics have heaped praise on the book, with Library Journal hailing it as “a love song to dance in all its forms and the city that invented and perfected so many styles.” McDougall spoke with us about taking a different approach to dance history, bringing readers into the immediacy of dancing, and how the texture of the dancers’ lives unconsciously affected the evolution of dance.
